summary: Piribedil is a non-ergot dopamine D2/D3 receptor agonist used in the treatment of Parkinson disease, both as monotherapy in early disease and as an adjunct to levodopa, and (in some regional labeling) for vascular/cognitive symptoms in the elderly. It is not FDA-approved in the US (used in Europe and elsewhere as Trivastal/Pronoran); this record is based on EMA/SmPC-style references. Doses are titrated gradually, typically up to 150-250 mg/day in divided doses for Parkinson monotherapy (around 50 mg/day in adjunctive/other indications). Key safety issues are sudden sleep onset (sleep attacks) and somnolence, dopaminergic impulse-control disorders, nausea/GI upset and orthostatic hypotension.
indications: Treatment of Parkinson disease, alone (early monotherapy) or in combination with levodopa
Adjunctive treatment of Parkinson disease to manage motor symptoms
Treatment of chronic pathological cognitive and neurosensory deficit symptoms in the elderly (regional labeling)
Adjunct in intermittent claudication of lower-limb peripheral arterial disease (regional labeling)

80-140 mg/day (e.g., 1 tablet of 50 mg per 100 mg levodopa), individualized

dosage.t: Once to twice daily with food
dosage.n: Use lowest effective dose in the elderly

dosage.d: Start low (e.g., 50 mg/day) and increase by ~50 mg every few days to the target dose

admin: Take tablets whole at the end of a meal with half a glass of water to reduce nausea
Titrate the dose up slowly and divide doses through the day
Do not stop dopaminergic therapy abruptly (risk of a neuroleptic-malignant-like syndrome)
Warn patients about possible sudden sleep onset before driving or operating machinery
Review periodically for impulse-control behaviors (gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping/eating)
moa: Piribedil is a non-ergoline dopamine agonist that directly stimulates dopaminergic D2 and D3 receptors in the striatum and other brain regions, partly compensating for the dopaminergic deficit of Parkinson disease. It also has alpha-2 adrenergic antagonist activity, which contributes to its effects on vigilance and the cerebral circulation. By acting directly on postsynaptic receptors it does not depend on endogenous dopamine synthesis.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to piribedil or any excipient
Concomitant use with antiemetic neuroleptics (dopamine antagonists) - mutual antagonism
relative: History of impulse-control disorder or compulsive behavior
Daytime somnolence or history of sudden sleep onset
monitor: Daytime somnolence and sudden sleep onset

preg: Use is not recommended during pregnancy because clinical data are limited; administer only if clearly necessary after weighing benefit and risk, per SmPC.
lact: Breastfeeding is not recommended; dopamine agonists can suppress lactation and there are insufficient data on transfer into milk.
renal: Data in renal impairment are limited; use with caution and consider lower doses, monitoring tolerability.
hepatic: Use with caution in hepatic impairment; titrate carefully and monitor for adverse effects.

major: Neuroleptics / antiemetic dopamine antagonists (metoclopramide, antipsychotics except clozapine) - mutual pharmacodynamic antagonism; avoid
moderate: Sedatives, hypnotics, alcohol and other CNS depressants - additive somnolence
minor: Other dopaminergic/levodopa therapy - additive dopaminergic effects (used intentionally as adjunct)
interactions.food: Take at the end of a meal to reduce nausea; no specific food must be avoided.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - it adds to drowsiness and increases the risk of sudden sleep onset.
interactions.diagnostics: No characteristic laboratory interference reported at usual doses.

common: Nausea, vomiting and other GI upset (especially during titration)
serious: Impulse-control disorders (pathological gambling, hypersexuality, compulsive shopping/eating)
emergency: Fall or injury from sudden sleep onset or syncope
Acute psychosis / severe confusion or hallucinations

monitoring: Excessive daytime sleepiness and sudden sleep onset (counsel about driving)
Impulse-control and compulsive behaviors (ask patient and caregiver)
Blood pressure, lying and standing (orthostatic hypotension)
Neuropsychiatric symptoms (confusion, hallucinations) especially in the elderly
counsel: Take with food to reduce nausea and increase the dose only as your doctor directs
You may fall asleep suddenly, sometimes without warning - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you, and avoid alcohol and sedatives
Watch for new urges to gamble, shop, eat or increased sexual urges, and report them - tell your caregiver too
Stand up slowly to avoid dizziness or fainting from low blood pressure
Do not stop the medicine suddenly; report confusion, hallucinations, or severe drowsiness
pk: Symptomatic effect develops over days to weeks of titration
Plasma peak ~1 hour after an oral dose
Supports divided dosing through the day (sustained-release formulations available regionally)
Store at room temperature, protected from moisture and light
pearls: Not FDA-approved in the US but used in Europe and elsewhere (Trivastal/Pronoran); this record uses EMA/SmPC references
Non-ergot D2/D3 dopamine agonist with alpha-2 antagonist activity - no ergot-related fibrotic/valvular concerns
KEY RISKS: sudden sleep onset (sleep attacks) and somnolence, and dopaminergic impulse-control disorders - counsel and monitor proactively
Titrate slowly and take with food to limit nausea and orthostatic hypotension
Avoid antiemetic/antipsychotic dopamine antagonists, which mutually antagonize the effect (domperidone is preferred for nausea where needed)
missed: If a dose is missed, take it as soon as remembered with food unless it is nearly time for the next dose, in which case skip it and resume the usual schedule. Do not take a double dose to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose may cause marked hypotension with cardiovascular instability, severe nausea/vomiting, and CNS effects. There is no specific antidote; management is supportive with cardiovascular and CNS monitoring, treatment of hypotension, and standard symptomatic care; contact a poison control center.
